title: Start a repo and make the first commit
summary: Turn a plain folder into a git repository, then move a file through the three areas until it becomes a permanent commit.
mental_model: Git has three places a file can be: the working tree (your folder), the index (the shopping basket), and the repository (permanent history). `add` moves a file into the basket, `commit` pays for the basket.

write.content:
# Aquarium Controller

Firmware for the tank controller.

steps.title: Look before you touch anything
steps.why: `git status` is the single most useful command in git. It tells you which of the three areas each file is sitting in. Both files are untracked: git can see them but is not yet responsible for them.
steps.expect: Two lines starting with ?? -- the code for untracked.

steps.title: Stage the README
steps.why: `add` copies the current content of the file into the index. Note the word *current*: if you edit the file after adding it, the edit is NOT staged. That surprises people constantly.

steps.title: See the split
steps.why: Now status shows two groups: changes to be committed (the index) and untracked files. This split is the whole point of the staging area -- you choose what goes into the next commit.

steps.title: Commit what is staged
steps.why: The commit records the index, not the working tree. notes.txt is still untracked and will not be in this commit. A commit stores a full snapshot plus a pointer to its parent.

steps.title: Inspect what you just made
steps.why: Every commit has a SHA, an author, a message and a tree. `--stat` shows which files it touched. Notice notes.txt is absent -- exactly as designed.

steps.title: See where HEAD points
steps.why: HEAD is a pointer to the branch you are on; the branch is a pointer to a commit. Three pointers, one line of output. Everything in git branching builds on this.

verify.label: README.md is committed
verify.hint: stage it with git add before committing

verify.label: notes.txt was deliberately left untracked
verify.hint: this scenario wants notes.txt out of the commit -- do not add it

pitfalls: Editing a file after `git add` does not update the staged copy -- you must add it again.
`git commit -a` skips the index for tracked files, but never picks up untracked files.
A commit message that says 'fix' costs a future colleague ten minutes. That colleague is usually you.
cheatsheet: make the current folder a repo with main as the first branch
compact view of all three areas
copy current file content into the index
record the index as a permanent snapshot
what did the latest commit actually change
